claims.text: Closely matched precursor decomposition temperatures cause nearly simultaneous reduction and atomic release of all metal species.
Nearly simultaneous atomic release promotes synchronized nucleation.
Synchronized nucleation minimizes local concentration fluctuations during nanoparticle formation.
Minimizing local concentration fluctuations promotes homogeneous alloying into a single-phase solid solution.
A broad spread of precursor decomposition temperatures causes asynchronous or sequential nucleation.
Sequential nucleation creates local elemental inhomogeneity and increases phase separation and segregation.
Sequential precursor decomposition can produce uncontrolled particle morphology.
Matched-decomposition precursors should produce nanoparticles with a robust single-phase solid solution.
Matched-decomposition precursors should produce a uniform elemental distribution.
Matched-decomposition precursors should produce a narrow particle-size distribution.
Mismatched-decomposition precursors should yield phase-separated and elementally segregated nanoparticles.
Rapid high-temperature processing followed by rapid cooling can produce single-solid-solution high-entropy nanoparticles by suppressing secondary-phase formation.
Conventional rapid heating and cooling without targeted decomposition control tends to produce phase separation, elemental segregation, and nonuniform morphology.
The synchronization mechanism applies to noble-metal HEA nanoparticles under rapid thermal processing.
Pt-Au-Pd-Rh-Ir is an example composition within the asserted applicability boundary.
Effective synchronization requires precursor decomposition temperatures to fall within a narrow window.
The acceptable decomposition-temperature window may depend on the particular noble-metal combination and its thermodynamic interactions.
Combining multiple metal elements can favor formation of single-phase nanoparticles.

contradictions.description: The query specifies nanoparticles containing more than five elements, but the only explicit example boundary, Pt-Au-Pd-Rh-Ir, contains exactly five elements.
The initial state is described as both dried and in solution; these states are mutually incompatible unless the solution is intended to describe a prior preparation stage.
